summary: Discusses an extension to a bridge protocol so changes in neighboring hosts' address parameters can be detected and disclosed across multi-LAN Ethernet systems. It addresses a growing problem as campuses and companies interconnect larger systems, and requests discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: When someone moves house, the mailman needs to find out quickly. This memo suggests a way for connected networks to notice and spread that news faster.

questions: how to make address resolution fault tolerant
what is arp in multi-lan ethernet systems
how do bridges detect host reboots
subtitle: Extending address resolution to detect host reboots in multi-LAN systems.

tldr.problem: In multi-LAN Ethernet systems connected by bridges, when a host reboots or relocates to a different network interface, other systems still hold stale address mappings, causing packets to be sent to the wrong physical Ethernet address.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal extends the bridge protocol to detect when a host's protocol address no longer maps to its previous hardware address. Bridges maintain global translation caches and emit "reboot packets" when they detect mismatches, alerting all other bridges and hosts to update their ARP caches.
tldr.outcome: This allows the network to automatically recover from reboots without invalid packets clogging the network. The approach favors transparent bridges over the "Agent" bridge model for better fault tolerance and self-stabilization.

today: RFC 1029 discusses methods for making address resolution more fault tolerant in multi-LAN environments. While bridges have evolved significantly since 1988, the fundamental insights about detecting topology changes and maintaining consistent address mappings remain relevant to modern network bridge designs.

sections.title: The Address Resolution Problem in Multi-LAN Systems
sections.content:
This RFC addresses a problem that grows more acute as interconnected campus and corporate networks expand. When hosts on different Ethernet networks communicate through bridges, they must translate between protocol addresses (such as IP addresses) and physical Ethernet addresses (48-bit hardware addresses). In a single LAN, Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) handles this. But in a multi-LAN system, bridges must forward packets between networks and maintain consistent address mappings.

RFC 1029 extends previous address resolution work by adding a mechanism for bridges to detect when a host's addresses have changed—either because it was given a new Ethernet interface (hardware reboot) or reassigned to a different logical address (protocol reboot)—and to propagate this information to all other bridges and hosts automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Big networks have many connected sub-networks. When a computer moves from one part to another or reboots, everyone else needs to know its new address. This memo explains how to tell them automatically.

sections.title: Bridge Operations and the Global Translation Cache
sections.content:
In a multi-LAN system, bridges act as intelligent forwarding points. Each bridge interface maintains a local cache of addresses seen on that LAN, and the bridge keeps a Global Translation Cache (GTC) of all <protocol, address, hardware-address> triplets it has observed across all its interfaces.

When a host on one LAN wants to communicate with a host on another, the bridge intercepts the ARP request. If the target address is in the GTC, the bridge can reply directly without cascading the request to all LANs. This reduces broadcast traffic and improves efficiency. However, if the bridge's caches contain stale entries—from a host that rebooted with a new hardware address—packets will be sent to the old address and lost.
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge keeps track of which addresses belong where. When it gets a request, it checks its memory to see if it already knows the answer. If a computer reboots and gets a new address, the bridge's memory is wrong until someone tells it.

sections.title: Detecting Hardware and Protocol Reboots
sections.content:
The key insight is that bridges can detect reboots by watching for inconsistencies. When a bridge receives any packet, it checks the source address parameters against its caches. There are three distinct cases: the source hardware address has changed (hardware reboot), the source protocol address has changed (protocol reboot), or both are new.

If a bridge finds that the source IP address is in its GTC but maps to a different hardware address than the packet shows, it has detected a hardware reboot. Similarly, if the hardware address is in the GTC but mapped to a different protocol address, it has detected a protocol reboot. Upon detecting either condition, the bridge creates and broadcasts a reboot packet on all remote interfaces containing the old and new address information.

All hosts and bridges that receive the reboot packet update their ARP caches and translation tables accordingly. This ensures that stale mappings are corrected automatically and immediately, without waiting for a timeout or manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: When a bridge sees that a computer's physical label no longer matches its old label, or vice versa, it sends a message to everyone: "this computer now has these new numbers."

sections.title: Transparent Bridges vs. Agent Model
sections.content:
The RFC discusses two approaches to bridge design: Explicit Subnets (where the host's protocol address encodes its network location) and Transparent Subnets (where subnets appear as a single network). In the Transparent model, some bridge designs use an "Agent" approach: when forwarding requests from one network to another, the bridge substitutes its own address as the source, acting as a relay.

RFC 1029 argues against the Agent model, especially for fault tolerance. If the Agent bridge relocates or crashes, or if the "Agent For Who" cache becomes corrupt, the network can become unstable. Instead, the RFC advocates for pure transparent bridges that do not substitute their addresses, relying instead on the reboot detection mechanism to keep caches clean.

This approach supports self-stabilization: even if bridges themselves reboot or move, the network will converge to a correct state through reboot packet propagation and cache updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Some bridges would pretend to be the middle-man, which gets complicated if the bridge itself breaks. Better to just tell everyone directly when something changes.

sections.title: Benefits and Performance Implications
sections.content:
The reboot detection and broadcast mechanism is more efficient than alternative approaches. Instead of each host individually discovering that a destination is no longer reachable and retrying with fresh ARP requests, the bridge proactively informs the network of the change. This prevents redundant transmission to dead or moved hosts, reducing wasted bandwidth.

The RFC anticipates that as multi-LAN systems grow larger and PCs become more common (many people power off their machines at the end of the day), reboots will become increasingly frequent. The reboot mechanism ensures that translation caches remain current, improving routing efficiency and reducing invalid traffic. This is especially important because bandwidth on remote networks can be a bottleneck.
sections.plainLanguage: This way, when one computer reboots, the network tells everyone else at once. Much better than everyone finding out the hard way by trying to send packets to the wrong place.
